name: Three.js
summary: A browser-oriented 3D graphics library that composes hierarchical Object3D scenes with geometry and material objects, then submits a scene and camera through renderer backends such as WebGL.

features.name: Hierarchical Object3D scene graph
features.description: Object3D instances maintain a parent reference and an ordered children collection. The fixed source exposes add/remove/traverse operations and propagates local and world transforms through the hierarchy, giving scenes a compositional tree structure.
benefits: Expresses spatial containment and transform inheritance directly
Supports traversal-based updates and rendering preparation
costs: Hierarchy depth and mutation order affect update work
World transforms require explicit matrix-update semantics

features.name: Mesh geometry and material composition
features.description: Mesh is an Object3D subtype whose constructor accepts a BufferGeometry and a Material (or material array). This separates vertex/index data from surface and shader configuration while retaining both under the scene graph node.
benefits: Allows geometry to be reused with different materials
Keeps renderable placement separate from buffer representation
costs: Correct rendering depends on compatible geometry attributes and material inputs
Separate resource lifecycles increase disposal and ownership work

features.name: Renderer scene and camera boundary
features.description: WebGLRenderer exposes a render(scene, camera) boundary and owns WebGL-specific state, capabilities, render targets, and resource management behind that API. The scene graph therefore supplies a common input model to a backend-specific renderer.
benefits: Presents a stable scene/camera submission model above WebGL calls
Centralizes GPU resource and pipeline state management
costs: Backend capabilities and browser context limits remain observable constraints
Renderer state and resource disposal must stay synchronized with scene resources

features.name: Modular loader and addon surface
features.description: The official documentation separates core classes from addons, including loaders, controls, postprocessing, exporters, and WebXR helpers. These modules extend the core scene and renderer contracts without making every integration part of the core package surface.
benefits: Keeps optional format and platform integrations independently adoptable
Makes the extension boundary visible to application authors
costs: Applications must coordinate addon versions and resource contracts
Optional modules widen the number of integration paths to validate

mathematical_views.model: Rooted scene graph with transform propagation
mathematical_views.question: How do parent-child edges and local transforms determine the world-space state submitted for rendering?
assumptions: Object3D nodes form a rooted forest or tree for the modeled scene
Each edge represents containment and transform inheritance
The model abstracts matrix and quaternion arithmetic while retaining update ordering

mathematical_views.question: Which scene resources and camera state are required to map an Object3D hierarchy into a renderer submission?
assumptions: Meshes relate geometry and materials to Object3D placement
A renderer consumes a scene and camera through a backend API
GPU command generation and shader execution are abstracted

mathematical_views.question: Where do optional loaders and addons attach to the core scene and renderer model?
assumptions: Core classes and documented addons are modeled as distinct module sets
Addon edges represent integration with core objects rather than historical influence
The documentation index is an inventory of public integration surfaces, not a proof of runtime coupling

benefits: Direct spatial composition and inherited transforms
costs: Tree mutation and transform propagation add ordering and update cost

benefits: Reusable data and independent surface configuration
costs: Separate resources create compatibility and disposal obligations

benefits: Backend-specific GPU state is hidden behind a scene submission API
costs: Browser and backend capability differences constrain portability

benefits: Optional integrations avoid forcing all applications onto one feature set
costs: Addon compatibility and lifecycle coordination remain application work
